## What an engagement looks like

Every engagement starts with a short call and a written note about the decision you are facing. We reply with a proposal that names one outcome, one team and one first cycle.

From there we work in weekly loops. Each week ends with something you can open, read or click, and a short list of open questions. You decide what moves forward.

We keep all drafts, notes and decisions in one shared place. When the engagement ends, your team keeps everything, and nobody needs us to find their way around it.

values.about-markdown-field:
## Who we are

Sample Studio is four people: a strategist, a designer, a writer and a developer. We have worked together for six years, mostly with small teams in education, public services and independent retail.

Each of us leads one part of a project, but nobody works alone. The strategist frames the question. The designer and writer shape the answer together. The developer makes sure it holds up once real people use it.

## How we work

We work in three short cycles. First we frame: one or two weeks to agree on the decision the work must support. Then we shape: weekly drafts that you can open, read and react to. Finally we deliver: a steady rhythm of builds, handoffs and review points.

Every cycle ends with something concrete and a short list of open questions. You always know what changed, what is decided and what is still open.

## What we believe

Clear questions save more time than fast answers. Visible drafts beat polished surprises. A result is only finished when your team can maintain it without us.

## Say hello

Most engagements start with a one-hour call. Send us a short note about the decision you are facing, and we will reply within two working days with a few questions of our own.

values.article-body-field:
## Begin with purpose

Most projects arrive with an answer already attached. A team asks for a new website, a dashboard or a set of templates. The request is sincere, but it hides the real question: what decision should this work make easier?

We spend the first days of every engagement finding that question. It is rarely the one in the brief. Once it is written down, it becomes a boundary for everything that follows.

## A worked example

Last spring a small museum asked us to redesign its events page. Attendance was falling, and the page felt dated. The obvious move was a fresh layout with bigger images.

We asked a different question first: why do people decide not to come? We read a year of visitor emails and sat with the front-desk team for two afternoons. The pattern was plain. People could not tell which events suited children, and they could not see prices before clicking through.

So the question became: how might a parent decide in under a minute whether an event is right for their family? That question changed the work. We added two plain labels to every event, age range and price, and moved them next to the title. The layout barely changed.

Bookings for family events rose over the next season. The museum kept its old design for another year, and nobody missed the redesign.

## Keep the question visible

A good question needs to stay in view, or it quietly slips away. We write ours at the top of every draft and read it aloud at the start of each review. When a new idea appears, we ask whether it helps answer the question. If it does not, it goes on a list for later.

This habit does not slow the work down. It removes the long debates about taste, because there is a shared test for every choice. It also makes endings clear: when the question is answered well enough, the work is done.

If you take one thing from this note, make it this. Before you choose a format, a feature or a tool, write one sentence that starts with "How might we help someone decide…". Then let that sentence judge everything else.

values.article-body-field:
## Draw the relationships

Every project has more moving parts than anyone can hold in their head. There are people who approve things, systems that feed each other and deadlines that quietly depend on other deadlines. Most surprises come from a connection nobody drew.

Early in each engagement we make a simple map. We list the people, decisions and dependencies that can change the path of the work, then draw lines between them. The map does not need to be polished. It needs to make the next conversation easier.

## A worked example

A regional library network asked us to help launch a shared booking system for its meeting rooms. On paper the job was a form and a calendar. The team expected six weeks of work.

We spent the first two days on a map instead. Boxes for each branch, each approval step and each system that stored room data. Arrows for every handoff. Within an hour, three problems appeared that nobody had mentioned.

Two branches kept their room lists in a spreadsheet that only one person could edit. Evening bookings needed sign-off from a facilities team that was not in the project at all. And the payment system renewed its contract two weeks before the planned launch.

None of these were design problems, but each one could have stopped the launch. We circled them on the map and gave each one an owner. The facilities lead joined the weekly review. The spreadsheet moved into the shared system in week two. The launch date moved by one week, planned in advance rather than forced at the last minute.

## Keep the map alive

A map drawn once and filed away is only a record. We pin ours to the wall and update it at every review. When a box changes owner or an arrow disappears, we redraw it in front of the team.

The map also changes the tone of meetings. People stop defending their part of the project and start pointing at the drawing. "This arrow looks fragile" is an easier sentence to say than "your team is late".

Try it on your next project. Take a large sheet of paper and give yourself twenty minutes. Draw every person and system that can say no, then draw how they connect. Circle anything that surprises you, and give each circle a name.
values.article-intro-field: A lightweight map can reveal where timing, ownership, and information need attention.

values.article-body-field:
## Share something concrete

Large reviews tend to go wrong in the same way. After weeks of quiet work, a team unveils a finished design. The room nods politely, then the real feedback arrives by email over the following fortnight, and much of it contradicts the rest.

We avoid this by reviewing small things often. A narrow draft gives collaborators a real choice to react to. Capture what changed, decide what remains open, and prepare the next useful slice.

## A worked example

A small software company asked us to rewrite the onboarding emails for its accounting tool. The first brief asked for a finished set of nine emails in a month.

Instead we sent one email in the first week. It was rough, with notes in the margin explaining each choice. The support lead replied within a day: customers never read past the second paragraph, so the key step had to come first.

That single comment reshaped all nine emails. We rewrote the first one, reviewed it again, then drafted the next two using the same pattern. Each week brought a small batch and a short call. By week four the set was done, and the support lead had shaped every one of them.

Had we delivered all nine at once, we would have repeated the same mistake nine times.

## Make each loop count

Small loops only work when each one is focused. We keep three rules for every review.

First, share one thing at a time, and say what kind of feedback you need. "Is the order right?" gets better answers than "What do you think?".

Second, write down what was decided before the call ends. A short list of decisions and open questions stops the same topic from returning next week.

Third, keep the loop short. We aim for a week between drafts, and never more than two. A long gap lets assumptions grow unnoticed.

This rhythm asks for a little trust at the start, because early drafts look unfinished. Most teams find it calmer than the big reveal, because nobody is ever far from agreement.
values.article-intro-field: Small reviews turn abstract agreement into specific, timely feedback.
